verdict.headline: Houthis claim strikes on Saudi oil export sites as markets wait for Sunday's oil open
verdict.label: Sunday: S&P 500 closed Fri at 7,623.68 (-0.52%), Nasdaq 25,955.34 (-0.21%), Dow 52,215.16 (-1.23%); 10Y 4.999%; Brent $116.72 Fri settle (+6.2% on the week); BTC ~$80,414 Sun (-0.46% in 24h).
verdict.horizon: Sunday evening's oil and futures open through Thursday October 29, after the Fed decision and Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon results
verdict.rationale_short:
What happened: no stock, bond or oil market has traded since Friday, when the Dow fell 1.23% to 52,215.16, the S&P 500 0.52% to 7,623.68 and the Nasdaq 0.21% to 25,955.34. Brent settled at $116.72, its highest close since April 29 and up 6.2% on the week, and the 10-year ended at 4.999%. Over the weekend the Houthis claimed attacks on Aramco's Yanbu facilities, the Rabigh refinery and the East-West pipeline; the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted two missiles aimed at Yanbu and Taif, and neither Saudi Arabia nor Aramco had confirmed damage as of early Sunday. Bitcoin, the only market trading, was near $80,414, down 0.46% in 24 hours.

What it means: Yanbu is the Red Sea port Saudi Arabia has relied on for most of its crude exports since Hormuz closed in July, so a claim against it targets the route that has kept Saudi oil moving. The evidence points both ways: the Houthis have claimed many strikes this month, and none of this round's damage is confirmed. If nothing is confirmed, Friday's $116.72 already carries a large risk premium; if Aramco reports an outage, it may not be enough. Bitcoin has hovered either side of its $80,320 October 8 low all weekend without a clear break, which on thin trading says little.

What would change the picture: confirmed damage at Yanbu or on the pipeline would add to oil's premium at the 6pm ET open. Brent opening well below $113 would show the claims treated as contained. A 10-year above 5.11% with Brent above $113 before Wednesday's Fed decision would show oil-driven inflation setting rates; a 10-year below 4.95% would show growth and AI-spending worry back in charge. Conviction is low because no market has reopened and this run could check its sources only through search results.
verdict.lede_short: The Houthis claimed weekend strikes on Saudi Arabia's Yanbu export facilities, Rabigh refinery and East-West pipeline, but no damage had been confirmed by Sunday morning. Yanbu has carried most Saudi crude exports since Hormuz closed, so oil's 6pm ET reopen from $116.72 is the first real test. Confirmed damage would add to the premium; Brent well below $113 would show the claims treated as contained before Wednesday's Fed decision.

supporting_data.label: The Houthis claimed attacks on Aramco's Yanbu facilities, the Rabigh refinery and the East-West pipeline, while the coalition said it intercepted two missiles aimed at Yanbu and Taif — no damage was confirmed by early Sunday, so the claims are not yet a supply loss.
Brent settled Friday at $116.72, its highest since April 29, after a 6.2% weekly gain — that is the price oil reopens from at 6pm ET Sunday, and it already carries three weeks of rising risk.

The Fed decides on Wednesday, with Microsoft and Alphabet reporting that evening, Amazon on Thursday, and September PCE inflation and third-quarter GDP also due — the two forces behind October's moves, oil-driven inflation and AI spending, meet in the same three days.
The 10-year ended Friday at 4.999%, about 11 basis points lower on the week — bonds have not yet treated the oil rise as an inflation problem, which is what Wednesday's Fed statement could change.

Bitcoin was near $80,414 on Sunday morning, down 0.46% in 24 hours, between a $79,232 Saturday low and a $81,029 overnight high — it has crossed its $80,320 October 8 low both ways without a clear break.
The Dow fell 1.23% to 52,215.16 on Friday while the Nasdaq slipped 0.21% — the selling had spread from AI stocks to the wider market as oil rose, and that is where Monday starts.
